evidence.label: Single-exponential recovery and bounded-price strictness for metric k-median
The approximation threshold for metric k-median

headline: The best possible guarantee for placing k facilities is exactly 1 + 2/e, assuming P ≠ NP.
scope: It covers finite metrics with rational distances and separately listed candidate sites. The matching floor assumes P ≠ NP.
plain: In metric k-median you open at most k facilities to make clients' total distance to the nearest one smallest. Fast methods can only promise to land within some factor of the best total. Before this work that factor was about 2, and nothing below about 1.736 was possible unless P = NP. This paper proves a fast method for every factor above 1 + 2/e, about 1.736 (Lean proof listed). So 1 + 2/e is exactly the best possible factor, assuming P ≠ NP.
doesNot: This does not give a method that reaches factor 1 + 2/e itself. It also leaves open the version where facilities must sit at clients.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Charikar, Guha, Tardos and Shmoys, first constant-factor approximation
scorecard.significanceWhy: If it holds, it settles the best possible guarantee for a classic clustering problem. It closes the gap between about 1.736 and 2.

visual.title: Best proven approximation factor for metric k-median
visual.note: Smaller is better. Below 1 + 2/e ≈ 1.736 is impossible unless P = NP. Values ignore the small + ε.

explanation:
Picture a town with four houses and three possible clinic sites, A, B and C. The town can afford two clinics. Site A is close to houses 1 and 2. Site B is close to houses 3 and 4. Site C is close to houses 2 and 3. Close means a distance of 1, and far means a distance of 3. Each house uses its nearest open clinic. The town wants the smallest total travel distance.

There are only three ways to pick two sites. A and B give every house a close clinic, so the total is 4. A and C leave house 4 far away, so the total is 6. B and C leave house 1 far away, also 6. The best plan costs 4. The worst costs 1.5 times as much. This is the metric k-median problem. The k is the number of clinics allowed, here 2. Metric means the distances behave like real distances: a detour through a third point is never shorter.

Real instances have thousands of points, and trying every choice takes far too long. So researchers look for fast methods with a guarantee. Fast here means polynomial time: the running time grows like a fixed power of the input size. The guarantee is an approximation factor. A factor of 2 means the method's total is never more than twice the best total.

Charikar, Guha, Tardos and Shmoys gave the first fast method with a fixed factor, published in 2002. A local search method of Arya and coauthors reached 3 plus ε in 2004. Here ε means any small positive number chosen in advance. In 2016, Li and Svensson showed that a few extra clinics can later be removed at a tiny extra cost. That opened a route past factor 3. Byrka and coauthors reached 2.675 plus ε. Gowda and coauthors reached 2.613 in 2023. Cohen-Addad and coauthors reached 2 plus ε, first announced in 2025.

There is also a floor, and the town example shows where it comes from. Suppose every site is either close or far from every house. If the chosen sites leave c of m houses close, the total is 3m − 2c. A perfect choice gives m. Uriel Feige's 1998 work on covering problems supplies a hard case, assuming P ≠ NP. That is the standard belief that some problems with easy-to-check answers have no fast solution. Under it, no fast method can tell apart two cases. In one, a perfect choice exists. In the other, every choice leaves about 36.8 percent of houses far. That share is 1/e, where e is about 2.71828. The second case has a total of at least about 1.7358m, or 1 + 2/e times m. So no fast method can promise a factor below 1 + 2/e. That left a gap between about 1.7358 and 2.

The hard part is the clinic budget. A low total is much easier to reach when a few extra clinics are allowed. A 2026 graph-based rounding method also reached 2 plus ε. Its general transfer step stalls at factor 2 for this problem. This paper keeps the extra-clinics route. It first allows a fixed number of extra clinics, then removes them with the Li and Svensson step. Its new ingredient is a sharper way to compare costs while partial choices are rounded into whole ones. That comparison is what gets below 2.

This paper proves the matching upper bound (Lean proof listed). For every fixed ε, a fast method opens at most k sites. Its total stays within 1 + 2/e + ε times the best. It is deterministic: it uses no coin flips and gives the same answer every run. Together with the floor, the best possible factor is exactly 1 + 2/e, assuming P ≠ NP. Back in the town, the best total is 4. So the method's total is at most about 6.94, plus a sliver for ε. No fast method can promise to beat 1 + 2/e on every town.

The result has limits worth keeping in view. It does not give a method with factor exactly 1 + 2/e. Each ε gets its own method, and the power in its running time may depend on ε. The candidate sites are listed separately from the houses. The version where clinics must sit at houses is a different question. A companion paper gives a separate method that flips coins and beats factor 2 by a fixed amount. Its proof does not use the main paper's rounding argument.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked formal versions of four statements. Two are the deterministic 1 + 2/e + ε method and the exact threshold assuming P ≠ NP. The other two are the companion's coin-flipping method and its recovery theorem. Each has a Comparator statement listed. No specialist review has been published yet.
hypeCheck: Major if the proofs hold. Lean formalizations are listed for the main statements. Still, the threshold assumes P ≠ NP, and the guarantee holds only above 1 + 2/e. No specialist review has been published.

glossary.meaning: Choose at most k facilities from a list so that the total distance from clients to their nearest chosen facility is smallest.
A way of measuring distance where a detour through a third point is never shorter than going direct.
A running time that grows like a fixed power of the input size; this is what fast means here.
A promise that a method's total is never more than this many times the best possible total.
The widely believed conjecture that some problems with easy-to-check answers have no fast solution.
A method that uses no random choices and gives the same answer every time.
The exact boundary: every factor above it is reachable by a fast method, and none below it is, under P ≠ NP.
